# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v14)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod attendance); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—around sunset); present day (spring transitioning to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford harbor towns, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere); Secondary locations: San Francisco, New York, Eastern Prussia, Germany, Hamburgh; French locations (D——, Manosque, Sisteron, Hautes-Alpes, Paris, Italy, Durance, Château-Arnoux, Senez, Briançon, Aix, Draguignan, Embrun, Chastelar, Arche, Barcelonette, Jauziers, Tuiles, Joug-de-l'Aigle, Ubaye, Ubayette, Ollioules, Nice, Piédmont, Couloubrieux, Cannes, Rue Cassette, Elmhaven, Staveford, Grenoble, Bras d'Asse, Escoublon)
- **October 1815, early month, D——: About one hour before sunset, a man entered town on foot. Atmosphere: rain threatening since morning but holding off; frost silvered hedges overnight; chalked sun on forge wall; gulls quarreling over fish heads; salt and tar smell on wind; smoke lying flat; bell for vespers ringing thinly; baker's boy late, line at oven long; thaw left road rutted and puddled. At eight o'clock evening: Bishop at writing, Madame Magloire preparing supper, household about to dine.**

## Main Characters and Relationships

**M. Charles Myriel / Monseigneur Bienvenu / Monseigneur Welcome (Bishop)**
- French aristocrat; family ruined by Revolution; emigrated to Italy; wife died in Italy
- Became priest, then Bishop of D——; encountered Napoleon circa coronation epoch
- Redistributes entire 15,000 franc yearly State salary across 23 charitable categories; retains 1,500 francs yearly for personal sustenance
- Within less than a year, became treasurer of all benevolence; considerable sums passed through his hands
- Philosophy: society culpable for poverty and ignorance; dark soul results from darkness created by society; universe appears as immense malady with permanent fever and suffering everywhere; does not attempt to solve enigma but strives to dress wounds; tends permanent sadness seeking consolation; occupied only in finding best way to compassionate and relieve
- Attended condemned murderer's execution; spent entire day in prison; mounted tumbril and scaffold with prisoner; upon knife falling, told sufferer God raises the slain. Sufferer became radiant.
- Upon return, entered deep moral crisis: phantom of social justice tormented him; subject to lugubrious monologues questioning role witnessing state-sanctioned death; ruminated on scaffold as monstrous instrument.
- Daily life: Sleeps little; morning meditation one hour; says mass; breaks fast on rye bread dipped in milk; receives secretary and vicars-general; devotes remaining time to sick and afflicted; works in garden and writes. At eight o'clock evening, writes on little squares of paper with big book on knees; Madame Magloire collects silver-ware from cupboard near his bed; at this time he shuts book, rises, enters dining-room.
- Midday stroll in country or town when weather fine; often enters lowly dwellings; walks alone, buried in thought, supporting himself on long cane
- Presence warming and luminous; children and old people come to doorsteps for him as for the sun
- At half-past eight evening sups with sister: extraordinarily frugal repast of vegetables boiled in water and oil soup. When curés visit, Madame Magloire serves excellent fish or fine game.
- After supper converses half hour with Baptistine and Magloire; retires to write on loose sheets and margins. Man of letters; left behind five or six curious manuscripts including dissertation comparing three texts on Genesis.
- Called to bedside of sick and dying at any hour; understands this his greatest duty. Knows how to sit silent for long hours beside grieving widows and bereaved mothers.
- Household: ground floor three-room structure (dining-room, bedroom, oratory with no exit except through bedroom); alcove with bed in oratory for visiting country curates; hospital pharmacy converted to kitchen and cellar; stable in garden holds two cows; invariably sends half their milk daily to hospital sick
- Furniture sparse and austere: six silver knives, forks, and soup-ladle retained from former possessions; two large candlesticks of massive silver inherited from great-aunt; holds wax candles. Iron hospital bed with green serge canopy; bookcase cupboard with glass doors. Two oval-framed portraits: Abbé of Chaliot and Abbé Tourteau (appointed by king April 27, 1785).
- Red brick chambers washed weekly; exquisite cleanliness—sole luxury permitted.
- Garden: four alleys in cross-form radiating from tank with circumferential walk skirting white enclosing wall. Three plots used by Madame Magloire for vegetables; fourth planted by Bishop with flowers and few fruit-trees. Bishop plants and tends flower-beds; loves flowers.
- House has no locked doors day or night; any passer-by can push open at any hour. Philosophy written on Bible margin: "This is the shade of difference: the door of the physician should never be shut, the door of the priest should always be open." When asked about risk of misfortune, replied: "Nisi Dominus custodierit domum, in vanum vigilant qui custodiunt eam," Unless the Lord guard the house, in vain do they watch who guard it.
- **Bandit incident: After destruction of Gaspard Bès's band in Ollioules gorges, lieutenant Cravatte took refuge in mountains near Barcelonette. Bishop arrived at Chastelar. Mayor urged him to retrace steps; Bishop replied: "What would they say to bishop who was afraid?" Traveled alone without sister or Magloire; encountered no one; remained fortnight preaching, administering sacrament, teaching. Upon return, large chest deposited by two unknown horsemen containing pontifical vestments stolen month previously from Notre Dame d'Embrun treasury. Paper read: "From Cravatte to Monseigneur Bienvenu."**
- **1809: Summoned by Napoleon to synod of bishops of France and Italy at Paris (Pope arrested July 5-6)**
- **1811 (June 15): Attended synod at Notre-Dame under Cardinal Fesch; attended one sitting and three or four private conferences. When interrogated about his influence, replied: "I embarrassed them. The outside air penetrated through me." At colleague's house remarked on luxuries: "They must be a great trouble. I would not have all those superfluities, crying: 'There are people who are hungry! There are people who are cold!'"**
- **Political views: Took little part in theological quarrels; maintained silence on Church-State questions. Would have been found ultramontane rather than gallican. Beginning 1813, gave adherence to all hostile manifestations against Napoleon. Refused to see him as he passed through on return from Elba; abstained from ordering public prayers during Hundred Days. Acknowledged character flaw: Had his hour of party spirit, bitterness, cloud. Was Royalist; glance turned away for instant from serene contemplation.**
- **1815: Reached seventy-fifth birthday; did not appear more than sixty. Not tall; rather plump; took long strolls on foot; step firm; form slightly bent. Had "fine head" but so amiable people forgot it was fine.**
- Character: Does not attempt to impart to chasuble the folds of Elijah's mantle; projects no ray of future upon dark groundswell of events; does not condense in flame the light of things; has nothing of prophet or magician. This humble soul loved, and that was all. Inclined towards all that groans and all that expiates.
- Thought of grandeur and presence of God; future eternity, strange mystery; eternity past, still stranger mystery; all infinities piercing through senses. Without seeking to comprehend incomprehensible, gazed upon it. Did not study God; was dazzled by him.
- Considered magnificent conjunctions of atoms communicating aspects to matter, revealing forces, creating individualities in unity; these conjunctions formed and dissolved incessantly; hence life and death.
- Divided leisure between gardening daytime and contemplation night. Narrow enclosure with heavens for ceiling sufficient to adore God.
- No systems; many works. Did not risk mind in apocalypses. Apostle may be daring; bishop must be timid. Felt scruple sounding too far in advance certain problems reserved for terrible great minds. Feared sublimities whence great men like Swedenborg and Pascal slipped into insanity. Took path Gospel shortens.
- Besides sister Baptistine, had two brothers: one a general, other a prefect. Wrote to both with tolerable frequency. Was harsh toward general for time because general pursued Emperor at Cannes disembarkation. Correspondence with ex-prefect brother, fine worthy man living in retirement at Paris on Rue Cassette, remained more affectionate.
- **Current evening (October 1815): Had just come from his cold room to warm himself by the fire; cordial face easily grew joyous, illuminated from below by firelight; does not take up remarks dropped by Madame Magloire about dangerous vagabond; raising cordial face toward old servant woman, asks: "Come, what is the matter? What is the matter? Are we in any great danger?"**

**Mademoiselle Baptistine** (Bishop's sister)
- Long, pale, thin, gentle creature; embodiment of respectability; never was pretty; whole life succession of holy deeds; acquired beauty of goodness
- Yearly income 500 francs for personal wants; subsists on shared 1,500 francs with bishop and servant
- Overheard and preserved Bishop's self-reproaching monologues about scaffold and death; witnessed his deep moral crisis
- In letter to Madame the Vicomtess de Boischevron reveals: Initially feared his dangers; now accustomed to risks. Makes sign to Magloire not to oppose him. Carries off Magloire, enters chamber, prays, falls asleep; at ease knowing if anything happened, she would go to good God with her brother and bishop.
- **Current evening: Desirous of satisfying Madame Magloire without displeasing her brother, ventured to say timidly (remark not yet recorded in excerpts)**

**Madame Magloire** (Bishop's servant)
- Only servant in household; grumbled about financial arrangement; likes to call Bishop "Your Grace"
- Subsists on shared 1,500 francs yearly; takes advantage of visiting curés to serve excellent fish and game
- Had frights from unlocked door but eventually accustomed herself to Bishop's openness; now shares confidence or acts as though she shares it
- Attends household cleaning; discovered paintings beneath washed-over paper; contemplates silver knives, forks, soup-ladle with delight daily
- **Current evening: While procuring provisions for supper, heard things in divers places. People spoken of prowler of evil appearance; suspicious vagabond arrived who must be somewhere about town. Those returning home late that night might be subjected to unpleasant encounters. Police very badly organized; no love lost between Prefect and Mayor. Wise people should guard themselves well, close, bar and barricade houses, fasten doors well. Entered room to collect silver-ware from cupboard near Bishop's bed at eight o'clock. Emphasized warning words about fastening doors.**

**Jean Valjean**
- Man of medium stature, thickset and robust, in prime of life; approximately 46-48 years old
- Appearance: Cap with drooping leather visor; face burned and tanned by sun and wind, dripping with perspiration; coarse yellow linen shirt fastened at neck by small silver anchor; hairy breast; cravat twisted into string; blue drilling trousers worn and threadbare, white on one knee, torn on other; old gray tattered blouse, patched on elbow with bit of green cloth sewn on with twine; soldier knapsack tightly packed, well buckled, perfectly new, on back; enormous knotty stick in hand; iron-shod shoes on stockingless feet; shaved head and long beard
- Entered D—— early October 1815 about one hour before sunset, walking on foot, traveling from south (possibly seashore); same route Napoleon took from Cannes to Paris seven months previously
- Appeared very fatigued after walking all day; drank from fountain at boulevard Gassendi and again at market-place fountain
- Turned left at corner of Rue Poichevert, proceeded toward town-hall; entered and left quarter hour later; pulled off cap and humbly saluted gendarme seated outside
- Proceeded to Cross of Colbas inn; warmed himself before kitchen fire with back turned
- **Innkeeper Jacquin Labarre sent child to town-hall with note requesting information about traveller; child returned with reply. Labarre approached him, revealed he had sent to town-hall to identify him, and stated his name is Jean Valjean.**
- **Upon hearing his name revealed, walked out choosing principal street, kept close to houses like sad and humiliated man, did not turn round.**
- **Wandered streets of town he knew nothing of, forgetful of fatigue while sad. Felt pangs of hunger sharply as night drew near. Glanced through window of public house, saw men drinking, landlord warming himself, iron pot suspended from crane bubbling over flame. Approached, seated himself near hearth, stretched out exhausted feet to fire; fine odor emitted by pot. Face beneath cap assumed vague appearance of comfort mingled with poignant aspect which habitual suffering bestows.**
- **Fishmonger in public house had encountered him that morning on road between Bras d'Asse and Escoublon; Valjean had requested ride on crupper; fishmonger declined by redoubling his gait. Fishmonger had been member of group surrounding Labarre at Cross of Colbas, related disagreeable encounter. From public house, fishmonger made imperceptible sign to tavern-keeper; they exchanged few words in low tone. Valjean had become absorbed in reflections.**
- **Later: Entered little street with many gardens enclosed only by hedges. Caught sight of small single-story house with lighted window. Peered through pane; within was large whitewashed room with bed draped in printed cotton stuff, cradle in corner, few wooden chairs, double-barrelled gun on wall. Table spread in centre; copper lamp illuminated coarse white linen tablecloth, pewter jug shining like silver filled with wine, brown smoking soup-tureen. At table sat man of about forty, merry and open countenance, dandling little child on knees. Close by very young woman nursing another child. Father laughing, child laughing, mother smiling. Stranger paused in reverie before this tender calming spectacle. Probably thought this joyous house would be hospitable, and he would find perhaps a little pity.**
- **Encountered man of lofty stature, half peasant, half artisan, wearing huge leather apron reached to left shoulder, upheld by girdle with hammer, red handkerchief, powder-horn, all sorts of objects. Carried head thrown backwards; shirt widely opened displayed bull neck, white and bare. Had thick eyelashes, enormous black whiskers, prominent eyes, lower part of face like a snout; air of being on his own ground. With difficulty repassed fence, found himself once more in street, alone, without refuge, without shelter, without roof over his head, chased from bed of straw and miserable kennel. Dropped rather than seated himself on a stone; passer-by heard him exclaim, "I am not even a dog!"**
- **Walked thus with head drooping. When far from every human habitation, raised eyes, gazed searchingly about him. In field before one of those low hills covered with close-cut stubble, which after harvest resemble shaved heads.**
- **Horizon perfectly black; not alone obscurity of night but caused by very low-hanging clouds seeming to rest upon hill, mounting and filling whole sky. Moon about to rise; remnant of twilight brightness still floating in zenith; clouds formed whitish arch at summit of sky, whence gleam of light fell upon earth. Man evidently very far from having delicate habits of intelligence and spirit which render one sensible to mysterious aspects of things; nevertheless, something in sky, hill, plain, tree was so profoundly desolate that after moment of immobility and reverie he turned back abruptly. There are instants when nature seems hostile.**
- **Chased away from family home; despised; arrived in town afternoon of early October 1815 and already excluded from multiple potential shelters**

**Secondary Characters**
- Malis Prydenridge: Born at Kelmere; folk called him "Quiet Malis"
- Havie Prydenridge: By trade a herbalist; born at Elmhaven
- Rovus Prydenridge: By trade a chandler; born at Staveford
- Luvie Prydenridge: By trade a weaver; born in Salcombe
- Gadrek Prydenridge: By trade a miller
- **Jacquin Labarre: Landlord of Cross of Colbas inn; man of consideration in town due to relationship to another Labarre who keeps Three Dauphins inn in Grenoble and served in the Guides. The Grenoble Labarre received Emperor Napoleon after landing; this reflected glory distantly on Cross of Colbas Labarre.**
- **Fishmonger of Rue de Chaffaut: Encountered Valjean on road; refused him a ride; reported encounter to Labarre and other townsfolk; made imperceptible sign to tavern-keeper from public house**
- General Drouot: Mounted stone bench at town-hall on March 4th to read proclamation of Gulf Juan
- Gendarme seated near town-hall door
- Old Member of the Convention (G——) [DECEASED]: Debated French Revolution's merits; voted for Republic; told Bishop "I am not even a dog!" upon deathbed confrontation with his choices; transformed in final moments

## Key Events
- Sir Felix exiled to Germany/Eastern Prussia before end of August
- Lady Carbury married Mr. Broune before winter was over
- Bishop attended condemned murderer's execution and entered deep moral crisis
- Bishop conducted extended deathbed conversation with dying old member of Convention
- Early October 1815, afternoon: Jean Valjean arrives in D——; identified by innkeeper Labarre; encounters fishmonger who reports him to others; attempts to find shelter in public house, single-family home, then farmyard; chased from each in succession; forced to seek refuge outdoors amid hostile nature; during all this, town folk gather spreading fear and distrust

## Themes
- Social rejection and systematic exclusion of mysterious stranger
- Hospitality versus suspicion; human dignity denied through appearance and reputation
- Desperate hunger and fatigue; human need confronting community indifference
- Contrast between domestic happiness and homelessness; family warmth as unattainable refuge
- Isolation despite presence of other humans; progressive narrowing of shelter options
- Physical and emotional degradation; repeated humiliation compounding each refusal
- Nature's hostility as mirror to human hostility
